nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer of the Georgia backcountry, a Roman Catholic whose comic and violent stories of the action of grace - 'A Good Man Is Hard to Find', 'Good Country People' - are among the most admired in the language
biography: Mary Flannery O'Connor was born in Savannah, Georgia, on 25 March 1925, the only child of Edward Francis O'Connor and Regina Cline; the family moved to Milledgeville in 1940, her father died of lupus in 1941, and she took her degree at Georgia State College for Women in 1945 and studied at the Iowa Writers' Workshop, where she took her MFA in 1947. She wrote Wise Blood (1952) and The Violent Bear It Away (1960), the stories of A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (1955) and Everything That Rises Must Converge (1965, posthumous), the essays and lectures of Mystery and Manners (1969) and the letters of The Habit of Being (1979). In 1950 she was diagnosed with disseminated lupus, the disease that had killed her father, and lived for the rest of her life at her mother's farm at Andalusia, near Milledgeville, raising peacocks and writing in the mornings; she died on 3 August 1964, at 39, and The Complete Stories won the National Book Award in 1972.
literary_profile: Novels: Wise Blood (1952) and The Violent Bear It Away (1960). Stories: A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories (1955), Everything That Rises Must Converge (1965) and The Complete Stories (1971). Non-fiction: Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose (1969) and The Habit of Being: Letters (1979), with the early stories in The Geranium: A Collection of Short Stories (1975).
stylistic_characteristics: A comic, exact and mercilessly flat style in which grotesque events are reported without comment; dialogue that reproduces the idiom of the rural South with great precision; a habit of ending a story with a single turn that reverses everything before it; violent imagery used as the instrument of revelation rather than of sensation.
intellectual_concerns: Grace and the resistance to it, in explicitly Catholic terms; sin, redemption and judgement; the grotesque body and the disabled body; race and the American South in the years of desegregation; mothers and daughters, and the family as a field of violence; the pretensions of the educated and the secular.
historical_significance: O'Connor is one of the great American short-story writers of the century and the central figure of the Southern Gothic after Faulkner; her stories are standard anthology texts, The Complete Stories won the National Book Award, and her essays on the writing of fiction, collected in Mystery and Manners, are among the most cited by American writers on craft.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on O'Connor and from its pages on the individual stories, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the three Norton selections - 'Good Country People' (Harper's Bazaar, June 1955), 'A Good Man Is Hard to Find' (Modern Writing I, 1953) and 'Everything That Rises Must Converge' (New World Writing, October 1961) - so the two novels, the other stories and the letters have no records and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, essayist and activist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet of the Beat Generation whose long breath-lines and candour about sexuality, madness and empire made 'Howl' the founding poem of the postwar American counterculture
biography: Irwin Allen Ginsberg was born in Newark, New Jersey, on 3 June 1926, the son of Louis Ginsberg, a poet and high-school teacher, and Naomi Levy Ginsberg, whose mental illness and early death marked his life and his work. He entered Columbia University in 1943, met Jack Kerouac, William Burroughs and Neal Cassady there, was suspended and later arrested in connection with a stolen car, spent eight months in a psychiatric institute in 1949 at his own request, and moved to San Francisco in 1954, where he read 'Howl' at the Six Gallery in October 1955 and saw it published by City Lights in 1956. Howl and Other Poems was the subject of an obscenity trial in 1957, which it won; Kaddish and Other Poems (1961), Reality Sandwiches (1963), Planet News (1968), The Fall of America (1972, National Book Award), Mind Breaths (1977), Plutonian Ode (1982), White Shroud (1986) and Cosmopolitan Greetings (1994) followed, with the essays of Deliberate Prose and the photographs and songs. He was a public figure of the anti-war and gay liberation movements, studied with Buddhist teachers from the 1970s, and died in New York on 5 April 1997.
literary_profile: Poetry: Howl and Other Poems (1956), Kaddish and Other Poems (1961), Reality Sandwiches (1963), Planet News (1968), The Fall of America (1972), Mind Breaths (1977), Plutonian Ode (1982), White Shroud (1986), Cosmopolitan Greetings (1994) and Death and Fame (1999), with Collected Poems 1947-1997 (2006). Prose: Deliberate Prose: Selected Essays (2000), Journals: Mid-Fifties (1995) and the letters with Kerouac and Cassady.
stylistic_characteristics: The long breath-line: a line measured by the length of a single exhalation rather than by the foot, with parataxis in place of subordinate clauses; catalogues of people and things; a diction that mixes the prophetic, the obscene and the documentary; repetition and incantation derived from Hebrew liturgy and from jazz.
intellectual_concerns: Madness, confinement and the destruction of the gifted by American society; sexuality and the closet; war, empire and the military-industrial state; the sacred in the ordinary and in the body; friendship and the Beat community; Buddhism, chant and the discipline of attention; testimony, and the poet as witness.
historical_significance: Ginsberg is the most public poet of the American postwar avant-garde and 'Howl' the poem through which the Beat Generation is defined; the 1957 obscenity trial became a landmark of American free expression, the poem is a standard anthology and course text, and Ginsberg's readings, recordings and activism made him one of the best-known poets of the century.
bibliographical_notes: The biography and the list of books above come from Wikipedia's article on Ginsberg and on 'Howl', read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Howl' (written 1954-55; Howl and Other Poems, City Lights, 1956); the other collections, the essays and the journals have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist and theorist of the exhausted mode, the most programmatic of the American postmodernists, whose Lost in the Funhouse (1968) turned the short story into an essay on its own making
biography: John Simmons Barth was born in Cambridge, Maryland, on 27 May 1930, the son of a candy-store owner; he studied briefly at the Juilliard School, took his BA and MA at Johns Hopkins University, and taught at Pennsylvania State University from 1953 to 1965 and then at the State University of New York at Buffalo, before returning to Johns Hopkins in 1973 as Alumni Centennial Professor, retiring in 1995. The Floating Opera (1956) and The End of the Road (1958) are realist novels, The Sot-Weed Factor (1960) and Giles Goat-Boy (1966) mock-epic ones; Lost in the Funhouse (1968) followed his essay 'The Literature of Exhaustion' (1967) and made him the leading theorist of American metafiction, and Chimera (1972) won the National Book Award in 1973. LETTERS (1979), Sabbatical (1982), The Tidewater Tales (1987), The Last Voyage of Somebody the Sailor (1991), Once Upon a Time (1994) and Coming Soon!!! (2001) followed, with the non-fiction of The Friday Book (1984) and Further Fridays (1995). He died at Bonita Springs, Florida, on 2 April 2024.
literary_profile: Novels: The Floating Opera (1956), The End of the Road (1958), The Sot-Weed Factor (1960), Giles Goat-Boy (1966), Chimera (1972), LETTERS (1979), Sabbatical (1982), The Tidewater Tales (1987), The Last Voyage of Somebody the Sailor (1991), Once Upon a Time (1994), Coming Soon!!! (2001) and Every Third Thought (2015). Stories: Lost in the Funhouse (1968), On with the Story (1996) and The Development (2008). Non-fiction: The Friday Book (1984) and Further Fridays (1995).
stylistic_characteristics: Stories that interrupt themselves to discuss their own construction, with footnotes, diagrams, blank pages and alternative endings; pastiche of earlier genres from the eighteenth-century novel to the detective story; a prose of great rhetorical energy and comic pedantry; the repeated figure of the author as a character in his own text.
intellectual_concerns: The exhaustion of literary forms and the possibility of writing after them; storytelling as a subject in itself; myth, epic and the oldest stories reused; identity as performance and as quotation; the artist's career and the relation of a writer to his own earlier books; the comic and the cosmic.
historical_significance: Barth is the figure through which American postmodernism and metafiction are usually taught, and 'The Literature of Exhaustion' is one of the most cited critical essays of the postwar decades; Lost in the Funhouse is a standard text in courses on the American short story and on experimental fiction, and his influence on the writers who followed him - from Barth's own students to the metafiction of the 1970s and 1980s - is widely acknowledged.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Barth and on Lost in the Funhouse, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections of the title story, 'Lost in the Funhouse' (The Atlantic Monthly, November 1967; collected 1968); the novels, the other stories and the criticism have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist, novelist and screenwriter writing in English
literary_identity: American essayist and novelist whose cool, fragmentary reports on California and on American politics - Slouching Towards Bethlehem, The White Album - made her the most imitated prose stylist of American non-fiction
biography: Joan Didion was born in Sacramento, California, on 5 December 1934, into a family of California pioneers; she took her degree in English at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1956, won a Prize from Vogue for an essay and worked at the magazine in New York for eight years, and married the writer John Gregory Dunne in 1964, with whom she wrote screenplays and adopted a daughter, Quintana. Run River (1963) was her first novel; Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968) made her reputation as an essayist, and Play It As It Lays (1970), A Book of Common Prayer (1977), Democracy (1984) and The Last Thing He Wanted (1996) are the later novels. The White Album (1979) collected the essays of the 1970s, followed by Salvador (1983), Miami (1987), After Henry (1992), Political Fictions (2001) and Where I Was From (2003); The Year of Magical Thinking (2005), written after Dunne's death in 2003, won the National Book Award, and Blue Nights (2011) followed the death of her daughter. She died in New York on 23 December 2021.
literary_profile: Non-fiction: Slouching Towards Bethlehem (1968), The White Album (1979), Salvador (1983), Miami (1987), After Henry (1992), Political Fictions (2001), Where I Was From (2003), The Year of Magical Thinking (2005), We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Live (2006) and Blue Nights (2011). Novels: Run River (1963), Play It As It Lays (1970), A Book of Common Prayer (1977), Democracy (1984) and The Last Thing He Wanted (1996). Screenplays, with John Gregory Dunne, include Panic in Needle Park (1971) and A Star Is Born (1976).
stylistic_characteristics: Short declarative sentences and a deliberately flat rhythm; the repeated phrase and the returning motif as structure; juxtaposition of reportage and private recollection without transition; quotation of documents, testimony and song lyrics; a first person that is present but withheld, and an irony that never quite becomes judgement.
intellectual_concerns: California as a place and a state of mind; the 1960s and their aftermath, above all in Los Angeles; narrative itself and the stories people tell to survive; women's lives and the pressure of feminine roles; politics, media and the manipulation of images; grief, illness and memory.
historical_significance: Didion is the most influential American essayist of the last half-century and the model for the personal, reportorial non-fiction that followed her; The White Album was named by Publishers Weekly among the ten most important essays since 1950, The Year of Magical Thinking won the National Book Award, and her sentences are among the most quoted in modern American prose.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on The White Album and from general knowledge, checked against the article's publication details; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'The White Album' (New West, 1979; collected 1979); the other collections and the novels have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, art critic and editor writing in English
literary_identity: American poet and art critic, the most influential and most imitated American poet of the half-century after 1955, whose Some Trees and Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror made difficulty, digression and unresolved tone the working conditions of American poetry
biography: John Lawrence Ashbery was born in Rochester, New York, on 28 July 1927 and grew up on a fruit farm near Sodus, in the orchard country south of Lake Ontario, a landscape that recurs in his early poems. He was educated at Deerfield Academy, where he first read Auden and Dylan Thomas and had two poems printed in Poetry without his knowledge, and at Harvard, where he wrote on Auden, edited the Harvard Advocate and met Frank O'Hara and Kenneth Koch. He took an MA at Columbia in 1951 with a thesis on Henry Green, worked as a copywriter for Oxford University Press and then for McGraw-Hill, and in 1955 went to France on a Fulbright, remaining in Paris for most of a decade and writing art criticism for the New York Herald Tribune and Art News. Some Trees, chosen by W. H. Auden for the Yale Series of Younger Poets, appeared in 1956 and sold slowly; The Tennis Court Oath (1962) divided its first readers, Rivers and Mountains (1966) restored his standing, and The Double Dream of Spring (1970) and Three Poems (1972) established the meditative, disjunctive manner of his maturity. Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror (1975) won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and was followed by Houseboat Days (1977), As We Know (1979), Shadow Train (1981), A Wave (1984), April Galleons (1987), Flow Chart (1991), Hotel Lautréamont (1992), And the Stars Were Shining (1994), Wakefulness (1998), Girls on the Run (1999), Chinese Whispers (2002), Where Shall I Wander (2005) and later volumes; he was poet laureate of New York State from 2001 to 2003, and the Library of America issued his Collected Poems 1956-1987 in 2008, the first such volume devoted to a living poet. He died at his home in Hudson, New York, on 3 September 2017.
literary_profile: Poetry: Turandot and Other Poems (1953), Some Trees (1956), The Tennis Court Oath (1962), Rivers and Mountains (1966), The Double Dream of Spring (1970), Three Poems (1972), Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror (1975), Houseboat Days (1977), As We Know (1979), Shadow Train (1981), A Wave (1984), April Galleons (1987), Flow Chart (1991), Hotel Lautréamont (1992), And the Stars Were Shining (1994), Wakefulness (1998), Girls on the Run (1999), Your Name Here (2000), Chinese Whispers (2002), Where Shall I Wander (2005), A Worldly Country (2007), Planisphere (2009), Quick Question (2012), Breezeway (2015) and Commotion of the Birds (2016). Prose: Reported Sightings (1989), Other Traditions (2000) and Selected Prose (2004). Novels, with James Schuyler: A Nest of Ninnies (1969).
stylistic_characteristics: Long poems built of short, flat, syntactically exact sentences that change subject without warning; a tone that is courteous, melancholy and ironic at once, so that no single attitude can be assigned to it; abstraction and ordinary speech held in the same line; puns, clichés and quoted fragments used as materials rather than as jokes; prose poems and prose paragraphs in which the sentence does the work of the line.
intellectual_concerns: The mind as it actually moves, in fits and starts, rather than as argument or narrative would arrange it; the instability of the self and of the pronoun that speaks; painting, film and popular music as models of composition; the ordinary happiness and ordinary grief of American middle life; the impossibility and the necessity of meaning; age, memory and the deaths of friends.
historical_significance: Ashbery is the central American poet of the last half-century and the one against whom almost every later American poet has had to define a position; Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror is the only book to have won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and 'Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror' is among the most discussed American poems of the century. His influence on the Language poets, on the New York School's successors and on the conversational, digressive poetry of the 1990s and 2000s is acknowledged on every side, and he is a standard presence in anthologies and in the teaching of postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Ashbery, on Some Trees and on Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror, and from the contents listings of Notes from the Air and of Hotel Lautréamont, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the contents of the later volumes are given only in outline. Installment 10 records the three Norton selections - 'Illustration' (Some Trees, 1956), 'Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror' (Poetry, August 1974; collected 1975) and 'How to Continue' (Hotel Lautréamont, 1992) - so the other twenty-odd collections and the prose have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

literary_identity: American confessional poet whose five Houghton Mifflin collections of 1960-1969 and her readings made madness, motherhood, menstruation, adultery and suicide the matter of American poetry, and whose Live or Die won the Pulitzer Prize in 1967
biography: Anne Gray Harvey was born in Newton, Massachusetts, on 9 November 1928, the daughter of a woollen manufacturer, and grew up in Wellesley. She attended Garland Junior College and in 1948 married Alfred Muller Sexton, with whom she had two daughters, Linda Gray and Joyce Ladd; a third, Mary Gray, was born in 1955 and died within days. After a breakdown in 1956 she began writing poetry at the suggestion of her psychiatrist, Dr Martin Orne, and studied with Robert Lowell at Boston University from 1958, where she met Sylvia Plath; John Holmes and W. D. Snodgrass were early readers and advocates. To Bedlam and Part Way Back (1960) announced her subject: the asylum, the double image of mother and daughter, and the wish to die. All My Pretty Ones (1962), a finalist for the National Book Award, was followed by Live or Die (1966), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1967, and by Love Poems (1969), Transformations (1971), The Book of Folly (1972) and The Death Notebooks (1974). She taught and gave readings widely, performed with the jazz group Her Kind, and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. She divorced in 1973 and died by suicide at Weston, Massachusetts, on 4 October 1974, aged forty-five.
literary_profile: Poetry: To Bedlam and Part Way Back (1960), All My Pretty Ones (1962), Live or Die (1966), Love Poems (1969), Transformations (1971), The Book of Folly (1972), The Death Notebooks (1974) and The Awful Rowing Toward God (1975, posthumous). Children's book: Eggs of Things (1963), with Maxine Kumin. Posthumous prose and letters: Anne Sexton: A Self-Portrait in Letters (1977) and No Evil Star: Selected Essays, Interviews, and Prose (1985).
stylistic_characteristics: Short, flat, declarative lines that turn without warning into incantation; a nursery-rhyme or ballad music used for the most private material; startling similes drawn from the household and the hospital; direct address to the dead, to the body, to the daughter and to the reader; repetition of a single phrase as the spine of a poem; a spoken, performable rhetoric shaped by her reading voice.
intellectual_concerns: Mental illness, hospitalisation and the talking cure; motherhood and the inheritance of a mother's life; the female body, menstruation, abortion and desire; marriage, adultery and divorce; the wish to die and the guilt of surviving; fairy tale, myth and religion as frames for a private life; poetry itself as an act of exposure.
historical_significance: Sexton is one of the two or three defining American confessional poets and, with Plath, the writer through whom the poetry of the 1960s is most often taught; she brought subjects that had been kept out of American verse - abortion, menstruation, masturbation, psychiatric hospitalisation - into the anthologies, and her readings and recordings made poetry a public performance again. Live or Die is a Pulitzer Prize winner, Transformations is a standard text in courses on the fairy tale, and her influence runs through the poetry of the 1970s and through the later poetry of trauma and of the body.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Sexton, on Live or Die and on 'Her Kind', and from the contents listing of The Complete Poems, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the periodical first printings of the individual poems are documented unevenly. Installment 10 records the five Norton selections - 'The Starry Night' (All My Pretty Ones, 1962), 'Her Kind' (To Bedlam and Part Way Back, 1960), 'Sylvia's Death' (Poetry, January 1964; collected 1966), 'Little Girl, My String Bean, My Lovely Woman' (Live or Die, 1966) and 'The Ballad of the Lonely Masturbator' (Love Poems, 1969) - so the other collections, the children's book and the posthumous prose have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, essayist and feminist writing in English
literary_identity: American poet and essayist whose work moved from the formal verse of A Change of World to the documentary, feminist and lesbian poetry of Diving into the Wreck and The Dream of a Common Language, and who was for half a century the most influential political poet in the language
biography: Adrienne Cecile Rich was born in Baltimore on 16 May 1929, the elder daughter of Arnold Rich, a pathologist at Johns Hopkins, and Helen Gravely Jones, a composer and pianist; she was educated at Radcliffe College, graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1951, and in the same year won the Yale Series of Younger Poets with A Change of World, chosen by W. H. Auden. She married Alfred H. Conrad, an economist, in 1953 and had three sons; The Diamond Cutters (1955) followed, and Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (1963) - written over three years and initially ignored or attacked - began the turn towards the political and the personal that the rest of her work completes. Necessities of Life (1966), Leaflets (1969) and The Will to Change (1971) record the years of anti-war activism and of her marriage's collapse; she divorced in 1970 and Conrad died the same year. Diving into the Wreck (1973) won the National Book Award, which she refused as an individual and accepted with Audre Lorde and Alice Walker on behalf of all women. She came out as a lesbian in 1976; Of Woman Born (1976), The Dream of a Common Language (1978), A Wild Patience Has Taken Me This Far (1981), The Fact of a Doorframe (1984), Your Native Land, Your Life (1986), Time's Power (1989), An Atlas of the Difficult World (1991), Dark Fields of the Republic (1995), Midnight Salvage (1999), Fox (2001), The School Among the Ruins (2004) and Tonight No Poetry Will Serve (2011) followed, with the essays of On Lies, Secrets, and Silence (1979), Blood, Bread, and Poetry (1986) and What Is Found There (1993). She refused the National Medal of Arts in 1997, taught for many years at Stanford and elsewhere, and died in Santa Cruz, California, on 27 March 2012.
literary_profile: Poetry: A Change of World (1951), The Diamond Cutters (1955), Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (1963), Necessities of Life (1966), Leaflets (1969), The Will to Change (1971), Diving into the Wreck (1973), Poems: Selected and New, 1950-1974 (1974), The Dream of a Common Language (1978), A Wild Patience Has Taken Me This Far (1981), The Fact of a Doorframe (1984), Your Native Land, Your Life (1986), Time's Power (1989), An Atlas of the Difficult World (1991), Collected Early Poems 1950-1970 (1993), Dark Fields of the Republic (1995), Midnight Salvage (1999), Fox (2001), The School Among the Ruins (2004) and Tonight No Poetry Will Serve (2011). Prose: Of Woman Born (1976), On Lies, Secrets, and Silence (1979), Blood, Bread, and Poetry (1986), What Is Found There (1993) and A Human Eye (2009).
stylistic_characteristics: Lines that break where the thought breaks, not where the metre would; a documentary notation of dates, places and quotations; the long poem built as a sequence of numbered sections; the direct second person and the collective 'we'; images drawn from geology, cartography, medicine and the sea; an argument carried by the poem's own hesitations and revisions.
intellectual_concerns: The politics of gender and the institution of motherhood; sexuality, the closet and the love of women; language as an instrument of power and the possibility of a common language; history, war and the American state; race and the responsibilities of the white poet; the relation of the living to the dead, and of a poem to the world it intervenes in; art as work rather than as transcendence.
historical_significance: Rich is the most influential political poet in English of the last half-century and a founding figure of second-wave feminist criticism: 'When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision' and Of Woman Born are standard texts in women's studies, Diving into the Wreck is a National Book Award winner, and the refusal of the National Medal of Arts in 1997 made her a public example of the writer's relation to the state. Her influence on feminist, lesbian and documentary poetry in the United States and Britain is pervasive, and the later prose on compulsory heterosexuality remains central to queer theory's genealogy.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Rich, on Diving into the Wreck and on The Dream of a Common Language, and from the contents listing of the Norton critical Poetry and Prose, read directly; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the six Norton selections - 'Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law' (1963), 'I Am in Danger-Sir-' (Necessities of Life, 1966), 'A Valediction Forbidding Mourning' (The Will to Change, 1971), 'Diving into the Wreck' (1973), 'Power' and 'Transcendental Etude' (both The Dream of a Common Language, 1978) - so the other collections, the essays and the critical prose have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; Baptist minister, orator and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American Baptist minister and leader of the civil rights movement, whose sermons, speeches and prison letter made him the greatest American orator of the century and one of its most widely reprinted prose writers
biography: Michael King Jr. was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on 15 January 1929, the son of the pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, and took his father's adopted name of Martin Luther King. He entered Morehouse College at fifteen, graduated in 1948, took a divinity degree at Crozer Theological Seminary in 1951 and a doctorate in systematic theology at Boston University in 1955, the year in which he became pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama. The Montgomery bus boycott, begun after Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955 and lasting 381 days, made him a national figure; he founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957 and led campaigns in Birmingham in 1963, in Washington the same year, where he delivered 'I Have a Dream' on 28 August, in Selma in 1965 and in Chicago in 1966. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, broke publicly with the Johnson administration over Vietnam in 1967, and was organising the Poor People's Campaign when he was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, on 4 April 1968. His books are Stride Toward Freedom (1958), Strength to Love (1963), Why We Can't Wait (1964), Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? (1967) and, posthumously, The Trumpet of Conscience (1968).
literary_profile: Books: Stride Toward Freedom (1958), Strength to Love (1963), Why We Can't Wait (1964), Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? (1967) and The Trumpet of Conscience (1968). Sermons and addresses: 'I Have a Dream' (1963), 'Beyond Vietnam: A Time to Break Silence' (1967) and 'I've Been to the Mountaintop' (1968). Letters: 'Letter from Birmingham City Jail' (1963). Posthumous editions: The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr., ed. Clayborne Carson and others (1992- ), and The Autobiography of Martin Luther King, Jr. (1998), compiled by Clayborne Carson.
stylistic_characteristics: Prose built on the cadences of the Black Baptist sermon: long periodic sentences that rise through repetition, antithesis and parallel clauses to a declaratory close; quotation of Scripture, the Declaration of Independence, Aquinas, Augustine, Buber and Tillich as shared authorities; the parable-like example; the direct address to a named or implied audience; an orator's sense of the paragraph as a breath and of the list as a climax.
intellectual_concerns: Racial segregation and the moral obligation to disobey unjust law; nonviolence as method and as theology; the difference between just and unjust laws; the failure of white moderates and of the white church; the relation of American democracy to its own founding promises; poverty, war and the international struggle for freedom; suffering, redemption and the meaning of hope.
historical_significance: King is the central orator of the American twentieth century and the writer through whom the civil rights movement is most often read; 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' is anthologised in American literature, composition, history, law and theology courses and was reprinted about fifty times in college readers between 1964 and 1968 alone. It is a founding document of the modern theory of civil disobedience in the United States, its central sentence - 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere' - is among the most quoted in American public speech, and King's writings remain the reference point for every later American argument about race, law and nonviolence.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on King and on the Letter from Birmingham Jail, together with the account of the letter's printing history given there and by the dealers' and archive records consulted; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the sermons are listed by title and date only. Installment 10 records the one Norton selection, the 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (16 April 1963; first printed as a pamphlet by the American Friends Service Committee in May 1963 and in Liberation in June 1963; collected in Why We Can't Wait, 1964), so the books of sermons and the later essays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.
